title: On the diversity of material and immaterial forms
pass_a_gloss: Article I. On the diversity of material and immaterial forms. 1. So that the decision of this question On the origin of the soul may be easily understood, I will premise certain things concerning the diversity of forms, and concerning the varied causality and potency of matter with respect to the forms which are introduced into it or are educed from it. 2. First, therefore, it is to be held that there are three genera of effects which are produced for some certain end, and not randomly or by chance: for of these some are produced by the concurrence of all four causes, some of three, some of only two. By the concurrence of all four causes are produced corporeal substances, which cannot have any real being in the world unless two internal causes, namely matter and form, and likewise two external causes, i.e. efficient and end, concur to give them the act of existing. By the concurrence of three causes, namely efficient, matter, and end, are produced all accidental forms or accidents, and likewise all substantial forms, the rational soul alone excepted: by the concurrence of two causes, namely efficient and end, are produced angels and human souls: for angels neither consist of matter and form, nor exist in matter; and therefore they can have only two causes, namely efficient and end. But human souls, although they exist in matter, nevertheless do not consist of matter and form, nor are they produced by the power of the matter in which they exist: for since they are spirits, they cannot be produced by the power of any matter, as will soon be proved, but are created by God from nothing, and are introduced into matter, for the best end, namely the glory of God, and the eternal salvation of those human beings. 3. I said that accidental forms, such as whiteness, blackness, etc., are produced by the concurrence of three causes, because in order that whiteness have real being in the world, (1) some end or purpose must excite and draw the efficient cause to act; (2) the efficient must apply its power or active concurrence; (3) the matter in which, or the subject of whiteness, must concur and cooperate by passive concurrence to give that being to whiteness: and this it does by receiving the action of the efficient cause producing the whiteness, and likewise by receiving the whiteness itself and sustaining it. From the concurrence of these three causes hangs the existence of whiteness and of other accidents, but especially from the matter in which they are received, which by passive concurrence produces and sustains their being: and that because from the efficient and the end they depend only as to becoming (quoad fieri), but from matter or the subject they depend both as to becoming and as to being (quoad esse): for they can neither come to be without the concurrence of the matter in which they exist, nor can they persevere in the act of existing if that matter is removed: but if the efficient and final cause are removed, an accident already produced can persevere in the act of existing, as is clear from almost infinite examples. 4. I said that all substantial forms, the human soul excepted, are also produced by the concurrence of three causes: because in order that the form of a stone, for example, exist in act, (1) some end must move the efficient by metaphorical motion; (2) it is necessary that the efficient by its power in act dispose the matter of the stone to receive that substantial form; (3) matter must, in the genus of subjective cause, concur to produce and sustain that form: and that because that form depends on matter as to becoming, being, and operating; i.e. it can neither come to be, nor be, nor operate, without the matter in which it exists: but this dependence of substantial forms on matter manifestly argues that matter is the cause of the forms existing in it, not indeed an active cause, but a passive and subjective one, as they call it: for every dependence of something upon something as upon a prior in becoming and in being is an evident index of causality: but the human soul stands far otherwise; for after the death of the human being it both exists and operates outside matter: Therefore it does not depend on matter as to being and operating; nor does it depend on it as to becoming: and that because matter cannot by any power or causal concurrence give being to a spiritual substance such as the rational soul is, as will soon be proved, and therefore it is in no way its cause. Hence it follows that the soul is among the number of those things which are produced by the concurrence of only two causes, namely efficient and end: it is also plain that the soul is rightly called an immaterial form, or one independent of matter, whereas on the contrary all other forms, both substantial and accidental, are called material forms and dependent on matter: e.g. the form of fire, just as it cannot exist outside its matter, so also without it cannot heat and burn. The form of a brute, just as it cannot exist without its matter, i.e. the body, so without the same cannot sense or desire. But the human soul not only exists outside matter after the death of the human being; but also operates outside it, exercising acts of understanding, willing, rejoicing, or grieving.
pass_b_english: Second Exercise. On the origin of the soul and the propagation of sin.
Article I. On the diversity of material and immaterial forms.

So that we may settle the question of the soul's origin with a clear mind, I will first set down a few points about the kinds of forms, and about the different ways matter causes and receives the forms that enter it or are drawn out of it.

2. Hold first that effects made for a definite end — not at random or by chance — fall into three kinds, according as four causes, or three, or only two, concur in making them. Corporeal substances need all four: the two inward causes, matter and form, and the two outward ones, efficient cause and end, must join to give them the act of existing. Accidental forms or accidents, and every substantial form except the rational soul, are made by three — efficient, matter, and end. Angels and human souls are made by only two — efficient and end. Angels neither consist of matter and form nor exist in matter, so they can have no more than those two causes. Human souls, though they exist in matter, still do not consist of matter and form, and are not produced by the power of the matter they inhabit. Being spirits, they cannot be generated by any material power, as will be shown shortly; God creates them from nothing and introduces them into matter for the best end: his own glory and the eternal salvation of those persons.

3. Accidental forms such as whiteness or blackness need three causes if they are to have real being in the world. First, some end or purpose must stir and draw the efficient cause to act. Second, the efficient must apply its power — its active concurrence. Third, the matter-in-which, the subject of the whiteness, must concur passively and cooperate in giving that being to the accident: it does so by receiving the efficient's action that produces the whiteness, and by receiving and sustaining the whiteness itself. From these three the existence of whiteness and other accidents hangs — above all from the matter that receives them and, by passive concurrence, produces and sustains their being. Relative to efficient and end they depend only as to becoming; relative to matter or subject they depend both as to becoming and as to being. They cannot come to be without the concurrence of the matter in which they exist, nor keep the act of existing once that matter is gone. But if efficient and final cause are removed, an accident already produced can still persist in existence — as countless examples show.

4. Every substantial form except the human soul likewise needs three causes. For the form of a stone to exist in act, some end must move the efficient by what is called metaphorical motion; the efficient must, by its power in act, dispose the stone's matter to receive that substantial form; and matter, as a subjective cause, must concur in producing and sustaining the form. That form depends on matter for becoming, being, and operating: without the matter in which it exists it can neither come to be, nor be, nor operate. This dependence plainly shows that matter is a cause of the forms in it — not an active cause, but a passive, subjective one. Every dependence of one thing on another as on a prior in becoming and in being is a clear mark of causality. The human soul stands far otherwise. After a person's death it both exists and acts outside matter. Therefore it does not depend on matter for being or for operating, nor for becoming: matter cannot by any power or causal concurrence give being to a spiritual substance such as the rational soul, as will soon be proved, and so is in no way its cause. Hence the soul belongs with those things produced by only two causes — efficient and end. It is rightly called an immaterial form, independent of matter; every other form, substantial or accidental, is called material and dependent on matter. Fire's form cannot exist outside its matter, and without that matter it cannot heat or burn. A brute's form cannot exist without its matter — the body — and without that body it cannot sense or desire. The human soul not only exists outside matter after death; it also acts outside it, in understanding, willing, rejoicing, and grieving.
source_text:
EXERCITATIO SECUNDA
De Origine animae, & propagatione peccati.

ART. I.
De formarum materialium, & immaterialium diversitate.

1. Ut decisio hujus quaestionis De origine animae, facilis intelligatur, quaedam premittam de formarum diversitate, deque varia causalitate, & potentia materiae, respectu formarum, quae in eam introducuntur, aut ex ea educuntur.

2. Primo igitur tenendum est, tria esse genera effectorium, quae propter certum aliquem finem, non vero temere aut fortuito producuntur: nam eorum alia omnium quatuor causarum, alia trium, alia duarum tantum concursu producuntur. Omnium quatuor causarum concursu producuntur substantiae corporeae, quae non possunt habere esse aliquod reale in mundo, nisi duae causae internae, viz. materia & forma, duae item externae, i.e. efficiens & finis concurrant, ad tribuendum iis existendi actum. Trium causarum concursu, videlicet efficientis, materiae, & finis, producuntur omnes formae accidentales seu accidentia, omnes item formae substantiales, sola anima rationali excepta: duarum causarum concursu, videlicet efficientis, & finis, producuntur angeli & animae humanae: Angeli enim neque ex materia & forma constant, neque in materia existunt; ideoque duas tantum habere possunt causas, videlicet efficientem & finem. Animae vero humanae, licet in materia existant, non tamen ex materia & forma constant, neque producuntur vi materiae, in qua existunt: cum enim sint spiritus, nullius materiae vi produci possunt, ut mox probabitur, sed a DEO ex nihilo creantur, & in materiam inducuntur, propter optimum finem, videlicet DEI gloriam, & ipsorum hominum salutem aeternam.

3. Dixi formas accidentales, ut albedinem, nigredinem, &c. trium causarum concursu produci, quia ut albedo habeat esse reale in mundo, 1. Oportet finem aliquem, seu propositum, excitare, & allicere efficientem ad agendum: 2. Oportet efficientem adhibere suam vim, seu concursum activum: 3. Oportet materiam in qua, seu subjectum albedinis, concurrere, & cooperari concursu passivo, ad tribuendum illud esse albedini: hoc autem praestat, recipiendo actionem causae efficientis & producentis albedinem, item recipiendo ipsam albedinem, eamque sustentando. Ex trium harum causarum concursu, pendet albedinis aliorumque accidentium existentia, praecipue vero a materia, in qua recipiuntur, quaeque concursu passivo producit & sustentat ipsorum esse: idque quia ex efficiente, & fine, pendent tantum quoad fieri, ex materia autem seu subjecto pendent, & quoad fieri, & quoad esse: nam neque possunt fieri sine concursu materiae in qua existunt, neque possunt in existendi actu perseverare, illa materia sublata: at efficiente & finali causa sublatis, potest accidens jam productum, in existendi actu perseverare, ut liquet ex infinitis pene exemplis.

4. Dixi omnes formas substantiales, anima humana excepta, etiam trium causarum concursu produci: quia ut forma lapidis v.g. actu existat, 1. Oportet finem aliquem motione metaphorica movere efficientem. 2. Necesse est efficientem actu sua virtute disponere materiam lapidis, ad recipiendam illam formam substantialem. 3. Oportet materiam, in genere causae subjectivae concurrere ad producendam, & sustentandam illam formam: idque quia illa forma pendet a materia, quoad fieri, esse, & operari; h.e. neque potest fieri, neque esse, neque operari, sine materia in qua existit: ista autem dependentia formarum substantialium a materia, manifeste arguit materiam esse formarum in ea existentium causam, non quidem activam, sed passivam, & subjectivam, ut vocant: omnis enim dependentia alicujus ab aliquo, tanquam a priori, in fieri, & esse, est evidens causalitatis indicium: at longe aliter se habet anima humana; ea enim post mortem hominis & existit, & operatur extra materiam: Ergo a materia non pendet quoad esse & operari; at neque ab ea pendet quoad fieri: idque quia materia non potest vi aliqua, aut concursu causali tribuere esse spirituali substantiae, qualis est anima rationalis, ut mox probabitur, & proinde nullo modo est ejus causa. Hinc consequitur, animam esse ex earum rerum numero, quae duarum tantum causarum concursu producuntur, efficientis videlicet & finis: patet item animam recte appellari formam immaterialem, seu independentem a materia, cum e contrario omnes aliae formae, tum substantiales, tum accidentales, vocentur formae materiales, & a materia pendentes: v.g. Forma ignis, sicut existere nequit extra suam materiam, ita etiam sine ea non potest calefacere, & comburere. Forma bruti, sicut existere nequit sine materia sua, i.e. corpore, ita sine eadem sentire, aut appetere non potest. At anima humana, non solum existit extra materiam post mortem hominis; sed etiam extra eam operatur, exercendo actus intelligendi, volendi, gaudendi, aut dolendi.
